tree.text: Morrow StudioWork / 01 — Aster HouseNext — NocturneWork10AboutContact(Project 01 / 10)Hospitality — Identity, DigitalMargate, UK — 2026Aster HouseTwelve rooms on the Kent coast, booked direct.Year2026ServicesBrand identityWebsite & bookingSignage & printClientAster House, Margate(Overview)Aster House is a twelve-room hotel and dining room in a converted 1890s seed merchant’s in Margate. The owners came to us six months before opening with a name, a building and one commercial goal: fill the rooms without handing a cut of every stay to the booking platforms.We designed the identity and the direct-booking website as one piece of work. The brand a guest finds on Instagram is the same one that takes the booking, sends the pre-arrival email, and greets them at the door.The owners didn’t want the usual boutique-hotel look: no brass, no script logos, no stock lifestyle photography. Instead the system is built from limewash tones, one typeface, and photography shot in the building in afternoon light.Fig. 01The signwritten lintel over the front door, where the wordmark began.Fig. 02 — Key fob, room 7: leather tag, brass ring, the house figuresFig. 03 — Breakfast card, filled in at turndown and hung on the doorA hotel brand lives at check-in, not on the homepage.Fig. 04 — Room 4, numbered by the same signwriter as the lintelFig. 05 — Stair hall to rooms 1–6(Identity)A wordmark painted on the lintel, then redrawn for screen.The signwriter’s lettering over the front door became a single-weight logotype that also works at favicon size. Room numbers, key fobs, the breakfast card and the bill all use the same figures, so the signage does the job of the brand.Guest stationery is printed by a local press in two colours, so reprints stay cheap enough for a twelve-room hotel.(Direct booking)The old site sent guests to a third-party booking widget. We replaced it with a short booking flow on the hotel’s own site: dates, room, a note to the house, payment. The full price, including taxes, shows from the first screen, and there are no upsell steps.Every room has its own page with real photographs, the bed size, the view and what can be heard from it at night. Rates, the seasonal dinner menu and photography are all managed by the owners in a headless CMS. The confirmation, pre-arrival and post-stay emails use the same type and tone of voice as the site.Outcome: in the first season, direct bookings made up [X]% of stays, compared with [Y]% before relaunch.Fig. 06 — Booking, step two: the room page shows the full price for the stay before paymentPlay film — 01:24Sound onFilmAn afternoon at Aster House. Its portfolio lived in a 60-page PDF that was out of date the day it was sent. We replaced it with a website the practice can keep current itself.The audience is narrow: clients writing tender shortlists, planning officers, and architects deciding where to apply. Each needs to find comparable buildings quickly, so the site is organised around projects, not around the practice.There is no animation on the drawings and no carousel on the homepage. The pages are built like the practice’s printed monographs: wide margins, captions in the margin, and drawings given the same space as photographs.Fig. 01 — Brise-soleil, Hollis Road SchoolFig. 02 — Competition model, photographed for the project page(Structure)Every project is entered once in the CMS with its sector, location, stage, size and status. The index can then be filtered by any of them, so a council looking for completed schools under 5,000 m² finds them in two clicks.Project pages are assembled from the same set of modules as this case study. The practice adds a building by uploading photographs and drawings and choosing a layout for each, with no design or development time needed.(Drawings)Plans you can read at any size.Drawings are uploaded as vector files, so they stay sharp when zoomed and load faster than the old JPEG exports. Each plan carries its scale and floor in a caption, never inside the image.Drawings deserve the same space as photographs.Fig. 03Stanhope Library, west elevation. It had grown from a WhatsApp group to [X] members and needed to look like a club, not a training app.Most running brands borrow the language of speed: slanted type, gradients, lightning. The club wanted the opposite, something that would sit comfortably on a 10-year-old’s first vest and on a masters runner’s race number.Everything in the identity is taken from the track itself: the curve of the bend, the white lane lines, the numbered lanes and the clay colour of the surface.Fig. 01 — Club vest. The arc can be cropped, repeated or used as a frame, but never rotated. It is published twice a year by a small team of writers and ecologists. We designed the first issue and the format every issue after it will follow.The editors wanted a magazine that could carry long reporting and long photo essays without either one feeling like filler. The answer was a strict rhythm: text sections and picture sections alternate, and they never share a spread.Every photo essay is commissioned, not licensed. We briefed photographers to shoot in flat, overcast light, so the colour of the land carries the pages rather than dramatic skies.Fig. 01 — Issue 1, “The long view”. The only spread where image and text meet.Fig. 02 — Photo essay: a hay meadow left uncut for one yearFig. 03 — Photo essay: field clearance on an upland farmGive the landscape the whole spread.Fig. 04Picture sections run full-bleed across the gutter with no captions on the page. Captions are collected at the end of each essay.(Format)Each issue runs to 192 pages at 230 × 300 mm, printed on an uncoated stock that holds the greens without making them glossy. The cover is a single photograph with the masthead set small at the foot.The grid has two columns of text and one wide margin for notes, maps and sources. Long reads can carry footnotes without breaking the reading line, which mattered to writers coming from academic and policy backgrounds.(Typography)One serif for reading, one sans for the margins.Body text is set at 10.5 pt for long reading. As restaurant orders grew, the studio needed an identity and photography that would hold up on a chef’s menu credit as well as in a shop window.Ceramics brands often photograph pieces alone on seamless white, which makes handmade work look like it came from a factory. We art-directed every shoot around use: plates stacked mid-service, bowls with food in them, shelves in the actual studio.The identity is deliberately quiet: a lower-case wordmark, one stamp, and the clay colours of the glazes. Because each piece is different, the brand around it stays the same.Fig. 01 — Celadon vase, from the studio’s first restaurant commissionFig. 02 — Breakfast bowl, shot in afternoon light on the studio benchEvery piece is different. The brand shouldn’t be.(Packaging)Stamped by hand, posted without plastic.Online orders ship in moulded pulp inserts cut to the studio’s four standard sizes, inside a plain box stamped with the mark in iron-oxide ink. A rubber stamp costs less than one print run and means the studio never holds stock of printed boxes.Fig. 03Glaze detail. tree.text: Morrow StudioWork / 08 — KilnNext — MeridianWork10AboutContact(Project 08 / 10)Food — IdentityLeeds, UK — 2024KilnWood-fired bread and coffee, branded around the oven.Year2024ServicesBrand identityPackagingSignage & menusClientKiln Coffee(Overview)Kiln is a bakery and coffee bar built around a wood-fired oven in a former railway arch in Leeds. The bread sells out by noon; the coffee keeps the room busy all day. The owners wanted to roast and sell their own beans, and needed a brand that could move from a café counter onto a retail shelf.The oven is the business, so it became the identity: the mark is drawn from the oven’s arched mouth, the palette comes from embers and flour, and the signage is lit warm, at the colour of the fire.Specialty coffee packaging usually leans clinical: white bags, tasting-note grids, numbered lots. Kiln’s bags are kraft paper with one stamp, closer to a bakery bag than a lab sample.Fig. 01 — House roast, 250 g. Stamp colour changes with the roast.Fig. 02 — Cups and saucers in the oven’s ash glazeThe oven is the logo.Fig. 03Country loaf. It costs a fraction of short-run printing and lets the range change weekly.Each roast has its own ink colour, so customers can tell blends apart from across the shop.Play film — 01:10Sound onFilm5am: lighting the oven. Its previous website looked like a sales brochure for buyers: renders, lifestyle copy and a “register interest” form. Renters wanted three things it didn’t show: the price, the floor plan and when they could move in.We rebuilt the site around available homes rather than buildings. Every listing shows its monthly rent, bills policy, size, floor plan and move-in date on the first screen, with no form needed to see any of it.Photography is of real apartments on real days, not renders. Where a building isn’t finished yet, we say so and show the floor plan instead of an imagined interior.Fig. 01Availability page. Homes are sorted by move-in date, not by price or building.(Availability)Listings are synced from Meridian’s property-management system every hour, so a home disappears from the site as soon as it’s let. Renters pick a slot instead of waiting for a call back.(Floor plans)Plans first, photographs second.Every apartment type has a clean, consistent plan with room names, total area and orientation. We designed the exhibition graphics, the catalogue and the campaign, working with the curators from the first room plan.Design exhibitions often assume visitors already know the field. The curators wanted a show that someone who came in to shelter from the rain could follow, so every decision started with the label rather than the poster.The identity is built from three solid shapes in the depot’s original paint colours. They mark the three sections of the show, each with its own colour, on the walls, in the catalogue and on the tickets.Fig. 01 — Section two, “Objects”. Plinth labels sit at seated eye level.Fig. 02 — Section one, “Rooms”. Wall text is never more than 60 words.Write labels for the visitor, not the lender.(Catalogue)A catalogue that works as a guide on the day.The 96-page catalogue follows the route through the depot, room by room, and fits in a coat pocket.
